question_text: In 1981, an art historian named Ellen Smart published an essay arguing that a specific cognitive condition, one whose modern clinical name did not exist when the subject was alive, explained a paradox that had puzzled scholars for centuries: why the most powerful ruler of what was then arguably the wealthiest empire on Earth had a 24,000-volume personal library he had never read. Records show that he had books read aloud to him each evening, choosing readers partly for the quality of their voices. The ruler in question commissioned Persian translations of ancient scripts, founded a purpose-built city as a new capital, held interfaith debates, and died having signed documents his entire life without ever having read one. Who are we talking about?
answer_text: Jallaludin Akbar (Akbar the Great, the Mughal emperor)

question_text: A tour manager carried a cricket bat belonging to his twelve-year-old cousin X, an uncommonly serene kid from Tauranga, New Zealand, to the continental United States in late summer 2002. He discovered its utility at the front desks of a budget motel chain: the cricket-obsessed South Asian staff, starved of any connection to the sport in a country that had no concept of it, would exchange room upgrades, late checkouts, and quieter floors for conversation and throw-downs in lobbies. He left the bat in Detroit in a studio in November 2002. The guitarist Y who found and kept it later used it on an album cover because he believed it visually approximated an elephant's tusk. The album was recorded on equipment predating 1963 at a studio in Hackney, London. Its opening track, which has no chorus, was initially dismissed as OK by the guitarist's colleague, was originally saved for a Bond-theme submission that never came, and sounds as though it was played on an instrument that was not used on the recording, became one of the most widely chanted pieces of music in the world. The guitarist was eventually asked to write a Bond theme five years later, with a different collaborator. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X = Kane Williamson, Y = Jack White

question_text: In the mid-1970s, a towering Indian icon poured his wealth into a historical epic originally titled Raj Karega Khalsa. The script followed a young man resisting a tyrannical Mughal regime, but the timing proved catastrophic: just as cameras rolled, a nationwide State of Emergency was declared, and paranoid authorities viewed the anti-establishment story as dangerously seditious. Hoping to soften the political blow, the filmmaker renamed it using a warrior quote from Guru Gobind Singh: Sawa Lakh Se Ek Ladaun. Though it briefly cleared censors in 1976, the Chief Minister of Punjab, Giani Zail Singh, feared the film's depiction of government corruption would spark civil unrest. Despite the director complying with demanding edits, including changing the characters' turban colors so they wouldn't match a rival political faction, the state pulled it from screens. The financial wreckage was absolute, causing a staggering 35 lakh rupee loss. When his wife wept over their ruined finances, the creator, celebrated for his unshakeable fortitude, shrugged it off with a piece of Punjabi philosophy. Relief only arrived in 1979 through a wild political twist: at a social gathering, the filmmaker casually mentioned the embargo to the feared youth leader Sanjay Gandhi, who turned directly to Giani Zail Singh and barked a command that the film should be released. The multi-year deadlock instantly evaporated. Who is this legendary Indian icon?

Tucked deep within a protected national park stands an engineering marvel that scales the sheer face of a cliff: the 326-meter (1,070-foot) Bailong Elevator, officially certified as the heaviest and tallest outdoor exposed elevator on Earth. Environmentalists fiercely contested its construction, fearing that the massive mechanical vibrations would compromise the park's delicate, millions-of-years-old quartz sandstone pillars. These gargantuan natural monoliths achieved global pop-culture immortality when they served as the definitive visual template for the floating, gravity-defying mountains on an alien moon. What groundbreaking sci-fi blockbuster film features this breathtaking landscape?

In 1902, a British imperial administrator faced a cartographic problem: the geometric line drawn three years earlier to divide two colonial territories ran straight across the landscape with no regard for where people actually lived, grazed, or watered their animals. His solution was to redraw the line along tribal use patterns. When independence came in 1956, each successor state selected whichever of the two colonial-era lines placed the larger, more valuable coastal strip (the Hala'ib Triangle) under its control. The logical consequence: the smaller, landlocked territory, a 2,060 sq km patch of desert called Bir Tawil, fell through the gap. Because claiming Bir Tawil requires accepting the colonial boundary that surrenders the valuable coast, it remains completely unclaimed by either nation. In late 2025, the Sovereign Council of one of these nations reportedly issued an internal order directing state bodies to treat the coastal territory as belonging to its neighbor, a quiet concession that, if formalized, would dissolve this famous terra nullius paradox entirely. What two neighboring African countries are the parties involved in this unique territorial standoff?

X, a well-known businessman and polymath who became famous for never blaming others for his misfortunes, once publicly accepted full responsibility for the loss of his own eye, not because the surgeon was blameless, but because he had failed to research a newer operation with half the complication rate before consenting to the older one his family doctor preferred. The specific complication that developed was an epithelial downgrowth. The pain was severe enough that the eyeball was surgically removed and replaced with a glass prosthetic. Years later, the same man visited a major ophthalmology institute at a California research university and asked why they were still performing the obsolete version of the same procedure. The answer he received from the surgeon, delivered without apparent embarrassment, he subsequently used in a widely circulated lecture as his single most vivid example of how institutional incentive structures cause professionals to knowingly harm the people in their care. He quoted the surgeon directly, who had said: It's such a wonderful operation to teach. Identify X.

In 1970, India was tightly gripped by the Licence Raj. High-tech equipment was heavily restricted and required government approval to import. Yet in this exact year, a major Indian corporation spent 8 crore rupees, a staggering sum, on a cutting-edge mainframe computer, becoming the first private company in India to own one. ISRO and IIT Bombay would not acquire comparable computing power for another decade, and no other private company in India would follow for another 21 years. The company was not an engineering firm, not a technology business, and not a bank. Its core product was something Indians bought not for utility alone, but to transform the way a space felt, in a country where those decisions were multiplying fast as urbanisation spread. They used the mainframe's computing power for a single, very specific purpose: to build a custom algorithm for demand forecasting and supply-chain routing, predicting months in advance which quantities, in which tin sizes, would be needed at which points in a network of thousands of small-town retail outlets across rural India. The accuracy rate eventually reached 90-97 percent. That data infrastructure became the invisible moat that allowed this company to reach and sustain a market share of approximately 40-50 percent of its segment, a dominance it has maintained for over five decades. Which company is this?

The H.M. Coroner for the St Pancras district of London, a man who once told a naval intelligence officer he could reach the mortuary equally quickly by arranging to be hit by a bus, agreed to invoke his legal power of absolute discretion over the disposal of unclaimed bodies. The body he provided was that of a Welsh vagrant found near a major London railway terminus, dead from ingesting rat poison laced into bread. His name was Glyndwr Michael. A naval intelligence officer and his Air Force colleague furnished Michael with a new identity: a Royal Marines major named William Martin, complete with a fiancee named Pam, West End theatre stubs, a bank overdraft letter, and a briefcase of top-secret documents chained to his wrist. The body was sealed in a canister marked Optical Instruments, driven overnight to Scotland by a racing driver who was severely short-sighted and refused on principle to wear corrective lenses, and released from a submarine off the coast of a formally neutral country on April 30, 1943. The scheme had originated four years earlier as item 28 of 54 deception proposals in a memo comparing wartime trickery to fly-fishing, circulated under the name of the Director of Naval Intelligence but almost certainly written by his assistant X, who later became famous for something almost entirely unrelated to intelligence work. Winston Churchill's confirmation signal read: Mincemeat swallowed rod, line and sinker. The operation was called Operation Mincemeat. Identify X, who almost certainly wrote the original memo, and what strategic purpose was Operation Mincemeat designed to achieve?
answer_text: X = Ian Fleming. The purpose was to convince the Nazis that the Allied invasion would target Greece and Sardinia, not Sicily.

question_text: In 1992, a Croatian-Canadian survey engineer used specialized geo-spatial software to calculate the coordinates of a singular point X in the vast South Pacific Ocean that represents Earth's absolute oceanic pole of inaccessibility. Located over 2,688 kilometers (1,450 nautical miles) from the nearest rocky shores of Ducie Island, Maher Island, and Motu Nui, this desolate marine graveyard is surrounded by roughly 9 million square miles of open water. The location is so profoundly isolated from human activity that the closest sentient human beings to these coordinates at any given moment are not passing sailors or researchers, but the astronauts orbiting overhead aboard the International Space Station at an altitude of approximately 400 kilometers. This extreme isolation has made it the premier global dumping ground for decommissioned spacecraft, housing the watery remains of hundreds of satellites and the Soviet Mir space station. Identify X.

In the summer of 2000, at cricket's most storied ground, a towering fast bowler who stood six-foot-six found himself at the center of one of the game's most chaotic days. Across the cricketing world, he was revered as much for a single act of supreme sportsmanship as for any delivery he had ever bowled, having famously chosen years earlier to warn a stranded tailender rather than end his run and unfairly claim a victory. When this June Test match began, he stood as the highest wicket-taker in the history of Test cricket. Conversely, he was universally acknowledged as one of the most inept batsmen ever to represent his nation, carrying a career average that would settle below eight. Neither statistic could prepare anyone for the second day of play. An absolute collapse saw 21 wickets fall in just over 76 overs. The carnage was so complete and symmetrical that portions of all four innings of the match were compressed into a single Friday. Because of the frantic rotation of players, this man was required to both bat and bowl in each of those four distinct innings as they unfolded on the exact same day, a historical first that has only been replicated twice since. To cap off the anomaly, when the opposition went out to chase their final target, he personally claimed each of the first six wickets to fall. Identify the cricketer.

On the morning of February 22, 1983, Bill Scanlon arrived at a tournament in Delray Beach, Florida, and promptly had a crisis. His equipment sponsor Wilson had insisted he switch to a new graphite racquet. He practiced that morning with X, the only man in history to win the calendar Grand Slam twice, using the new frames. The session went so badly that X himself stopped and asked what was wrong. Scanlon replied: I'm just scared to death with these new racquets. He panicked, drove back to his hotel, retrieved his old wooden racquets, and walked onto court for his first-round match against Marcos Hocevar, ranked 39th in the world, without having hit a single warm-up ball. He won the first set 6-2. In the second set, Scanlon entered what he later described as a complete bubble of focus. At the end of the match, the chair umpire pointed to the scoreboard and remarked on what had happened in the second set. Scanlon replied: I had no idea. The achievement was entered into the Guinness Book of World Records and remains the only verified instance of its kind in the history of men's professional tennis. Identify X, and what did Scanlon achieve?
answer_text: X = Rod Laver. Scanlon achieved a Golden Set (winning a set 6-0 without losing a single point).

question_text: In the early 1950s, legendary auteur Satyajit Ray ran completely out of personal capital and pawned his wife's jewelry to shoot the initial reels of his groundbreaking debut feature film. Production ground to a complete halt for months until the visionary Chief Minister of West Bengal, Dr. Bidhan Chandra Roy, stepped in to rescue the project with a vital government loan. However, the state bureaucracy possessed no existing financial ledger or accounting category to fund independent, artistic cinema. To bypass the thick wall of bureaucratic red tape, officials executed a clever semantic workaround: they officially allocated the state funds under a completely unrelated budget, justifying the expenditure by pointing directly to the literal English translation of the film's title. Under which budget heading were the funds allocated?
answer_text: Public Works Dept (the film was Pather Panchali, literally Song of the Little Road, so the funds were allocated under the roads/public works budget)

question_text: In March 2001, the oldest badminton tournament in the world held its last edition on a surface that had been quietly destroying the knees of players for decades: bare concrete, partially cushioned with synthetic matting. One player endured it differently than the rest. After each of his matches, five of them before the final, often two per day given the format, he lowered himself into an ice bath to reduce the swelling in a knee that had already been surgically reconstructed three times since 1994, when during a domestic team championship he tore his anterior cruciate ligament and lateral meniscus simultaneously. He had no physiotherapist and no support staff of any kind, and described the week afterward as having been played in a cloud of pain. He entered the tournament seeded tenth. He beat the reigning Olympic gold medallist in the round of sixteen in under forty minutes, beat the world number one in the semifinals in the only victory he would ever record against that opponent, and won the final in forty-four minutes without dropping a single game. The following year the tournament switched to a synthetic wooden surface, which he never played on in competition. He had watched a man win this same tournament twenty-one years earlier and decided, as a young boy, that this was what he wanted. Identify the player.
answer_text: Pullela Gopichand (winner of the All England Open Badminton Championships in 2001)

question_text: The greatest painter X of 17th-century Spain died because of a small river island Y. In June 1660, he was dispatched to supervise the logistics of an event taking place on it, housing, catering, and decorative programs for hundreds of nobles from two royal courts across twelve staging towns on a round trip from Madrid. He returned to the capital exhausted on June 26, developed a fever on July 31, and died on August 6. His wife died eight days later; they were buried together in a vault that no longer exists, because the French army destroyed the church above it in 1811. His remains have never been found. The event he organised on the island was the formal transfer of a Spanish princess to the French crown in exchange for a dowry of 500,000 gold ecus, a dowry that was never paid, and whose non-payment Louis XIV used seven years later as the legal justification for invading the Spanish Netherlands in what became known as the War of Devolution. The island, which shares its name with a bird, is still there, in a river on the Franco-Spanish border, roughly 200 metres long and 40 metres wide. It has been uninhabited since the day of that transfer, except for the two days each year when officials from both countries meet there to perform a formal handover of the island itself, alternating sovereignty every six months, under an arrangement first encoded in 1859 and formalized in 1868 on that very island, making it the oldest continuously operating example of its specific legal form in the world. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X = Diego Velazquez, Y = Pheasant Island

question_text: The man (X) who led the largest community migration in ancient Indian history did so because he had predicted, on the basis of sixteen dreams, that the northern subcontinent would experience a twelve-year famine, and that the famine was a karmic consequence of the killing required to build the empire. He led twelve thousand disciples south. His most important disciple (Y), who had founded that empire at roughly age twenty and had spent the intervening years unifying the subcontinent for the first time, performed the former's funeral rites on a hill in what is now Karnataka, and then undertook the same voluntary death-by-fasting himself, a practice his tradition regards not as suicide but as liberation. A 6th-7th century inscription at the site names his disciple not by the emperor's name but by a monk's name: Prabhachandra. Several scholars, including V.R. Ramachandra Dikshitar and John F. Fleet, have argued this means the emperor identification was a 19th-century interpretive error by a colonial archivist named Lewis Rice. Identify X and Y.
answer_text: X = Acharya Bhadrabahu, Y = Chandragupta Maurya

question_text: To protect the shocking, paradigm-shifting final twist ending of his low-budget 1960 psychological horror masterpiece, Psycho, legendary director Alfred Hitchcock instituted an unprecedented, hyper-aggressive promotional campaign. He forced theater managers across the United States and the globe to sign strict legal contracts enforcing an absolute box-office policy that ran completely counter to the casual moviegoing habits of the era. Prior to this, audiences frequently walked into theaters midway through a screening and stayed for the next loop. Hitchcock put an absolute, iron-clad stop to this, deploying specialized theater lobby audio recordings and armed security guards to enforce the rule. What was the policy Hitchcock introduced?
answer_text: No Late Admissions Policy (no one was allowed into the theater once the film had started)

question_text: Tiebreaker: As totalitarian shadows lengthened across Europe in the late 1930s, an elite athletic administrator in Rome named Ottorino Barassi realized that a highly coveted international icon was in immediate peril. Competing factions and occupying forces were systematically raiding bank vaults across the continent, hunting not just for financial bullion, but for potent cultural symbols of global prestige to weaponize as propaganda. This specific object, a modest 3.8-kilogram sculpture fashioned from gold-plated sterling silver resting on a deep blue lapis lazuli base, depicted a winged mythological figure holding a decagonal vessel overhead. It had been lifted toward the heavens only three times in human history, serving as the absolute pinnacle of achievement. Knowing that a routine inspection of the city's central vaults would lead to its permanent confiscation, Barassi executed a quiet, unauthorized removal, wrapping the artifact in rough cloths and transporting it to his personal apartment. For the remainder of the global conflict, this ultimate symbol of international triumph rested inside a weathered cardboard footwear container tucked far beneath his bed, miraculously surviving multiple invasive wartime searches completely undetected. When global peace finally returned, the hidden relic was pulled from the dust and restored to the world stage, remaining the defining obsession of the sporting universe until a completely new design replaced it in the 1970s. What are we talking about?
answer_text: The Jules Rimet Trophy (the original FIFA World Cup trophy)
